O.outcome_detail: historical-thinking rubric scores for assignments

cells.quote: As WHP-sourced assignments were among the activities that the scorers reviewed, the Digital Promise team expected those assignments to score higher on the rubrics because of their focus on historical thinking skills. This expectation was met, providing further evidence that the rubrics are functioning in the ways they were intended.
cells.note: The study describes this as a small convenience-sample comparison; no numerical effect size is reported in the provided text.

O.outcome_detail: historical-thinking learning-opportunity rubric scores across dimensions

cells.quote: As WHP-sourced assignments were among the activities that the scorers reviewed, the Digital Promise team expected those assignments to score higher on the rubrics because of their focus on historical thinking skills. This expectation was met, providing further evidence that the rubrics are functioning in the ways they were intended.
cells.note: The text reports that WHP assignments scored higher on the majority of learning-opportunity dimensions, all but sourcing. The reported ICCs concern interrater consistency rather than a treatment-versus-comparison contrast, so they are not coded as separate cells.

O.outcome_detail: 30-item reading-comprehension multiple-choice post-test

cells.quote: Based on the analysis of two-way Anova, it was obtained that Fobs= 436.6268 is higher than Fα= 4.4071. Therefore, it is implied that the students taught by using HT have significant difference in reading comprehension between those taught by using TFSST. Based on the mean score, students who were taught by using HT obtained 77.5; whereas the students who were taught by using TFSST obtained 68, so it can conclude d that students who were taught by using HT is better than the students who were taught by using TFSST.
cells.note: The study used cluster random sampling to select intact classes, but students were not randomly assigned to treatment conditions.

O.outcome_detail: reading-comprehension post-test

cells.quote: Students having high reading habit have better reading comprehension than those having low reading habit,
cells.note: Reading habit was measured with a questionnaire and categorized into high and low groups; the study reports a significant difference but does not provide the corresponding group means in the supplied text.

O.outcome_detail: reading comprehension post-test

cells.quote: The result of comparing HT and TFSST by using two -way Anova shows that Fobs was 436.6268 while the Fα with the significant level of 0.05 was 4.0471. Therefore, it implies that HT is more effective than TFSST in teaching reading comprehension.
cells.note: The study used a quasi-experimental design with intact classes; the post-test followed six treatment meetings.

D.treatment: educational work recognized in payment and evaluation systems
D.comparison: educational work invisible in payment and evaluation systems

O.outcome_detail: faculty educator role identity and involvement in educational activities

cells.quote: “When educational work is invisible in payment and evaluation systems, faculty gradually redefine themselves as service providers rather than educators.”
cells.note: The study reports a qualitative contrast: recognizing educational work is implicitly preferable to leaving it invisible, which was associated with reduced involvement in curriculum development, educational planning, and pedagogical leadership.

O.outcome_detail: faculty retention

cells.quote: “With the increased compensation, faculty members are more motivated to stay, …, they may be more willing to teach.” (Participant 18).
cells.note: Participants perceived increased compensation as supporting faculty retention; the pre-HTP/lower-compensation comparison is inferred from the study's before-and-after framing.

D.treatment: educational activities explicitly acknowledged in evaluation frameworks
D.comparison: educational activities not acknowledged in evaluation frameworks

O.outcome_detail: willingness to engage in teaching

cells.quote: However, participants emphasized that financial incentives alone were not perceived as sufficient to ensure sustained engagement in teaching unless educational activities were explicitly acknowledged within institutional evaluation frameworks.
cells.note: The study reports a perceived conditional benefit rather than a measured effect.

O.outcome_detail: faculty-perceived prioritization of educational work in performance evaluation

cells.quote: “In my performance evaluation indicators for paying for services, there is no quality or quantity of education. It is the number of patients that determines the amount of my fee, not the quality of education, not the number of students, not student satisfaction, and not even the satisfaction of the education system.”
cells.note: Interview participants perceived that HTP-era payment and evaluation indicators marginalized educational work relative to patient-service volume; this was not an experimental or quantitative comparison.

D.treatment: HTP implementation and service-oriented policy priorities

O.outcome_detail: perceived organizational attention to clinical education

cells.quote: “Education was already secondary before the HTP, but after its implementation, it has been almost completely forgotten.”
cells.note: This is a participant perception of reduced policy attention to education after HTP implementation, not a measured causal effect.

O.outcome_detail: students’ clinical competencies

cells.quote: “Before the HTP, we had time to teach at the bedside and discuss cases, but now they have less, and students’ competencies have declined.”
cells.note: Participant-reported perceived decline; the qualitative study does not provide a quantitative effect size.

O.outcome_detail: time available for bedside teaching and case discussion

cells.quote: “Before the HTP, we had time to teach at the bedside and discuss cases, but now they have less, and students’ competencies have declined.”
cells.note: The study reports participants’ perceptions that available bedside teaching time decreased after the HTP; no quantitative effect size is reported.

D.treatment: HTP implementation and increased educational resources

O.outcome_detail: availability of educational infrastructure, equipment, and funding

cells.quote: Participants described several structural changes introduced following the HTP as creating conditions that could potentially support clinical education. These included improvements in educational infrastructure, increased budgets, upgraded clinical facilities, and the expanded presence of full-time faculty members.
cells.note: Qualitative faculty perceptions; the study reports perceived post-HTP improvements rather than a measured pre/post effect.

D.treatment: educational equipment and simulators made available
D.comparison: availability without teaching support or time

O.outcome_detail: use of educational equipment for clinical learning

cells.quote: With the increase in hospital revenues and the allocation of more national resources, some of it was given to educational equipment such as training simulators. This was good. For example, we got several new models for resuscitation and injection training. But there is no one to teach, the equipment is very little used. We do not have time to visit patients
cells.note: The quote directly reports that improved equipment was very little used because teaching support and time were lacking.

D.treatment: HTP implementation with increased clinical cases

O.outcome_detail: students’ practical clinical skills

cells.quote: “With the increased number of clinical cases, students’ practical skills have improved, students have more opportunities to see real patients and practice procedures,…” (Participant 6).
cells.note: Qualitative participant perception; the study does not report a quantitative effect size or specify the duration of the learning exposure.
